highlight: In 1929, Columbia pressed a 78rpm disc with a joke on it. Sheik Karana's "Khatabeh Arabi" is described as a parody of an Arabic sermon in a mosque, and the flip side, "Mobaheseh Arabi," parodies a debate between an imam and an ordinary member of the congregation. The performer, the record tells us, was a clown or jester at the court of the Qajar shah Aḥmad Shah (1909–1925), famous for imitating the sound of the karnā, the long horn. A one-man brass section. What I love is how everyday it is: someone looked at mosque life, the speeches, the arguments, the voices, and found it worth a recording session. If you have ever heard a comedian do an impression of an uncle's favourite phrases, you already know the pleasure. You can play it on the Internet Archive.

Here is a window onto how North Africa travelled through other people's imaginations. "Gems from Algeria" is dated 12 November 1909, a Victor disc sung in English by the Victor Light Opera Company, with ten credits that include Victor Herbert. Its catalogue tags are "classical music," "vocal," and, worth a gentle pause, "ethnic characterizations." So this is a light-opera company's take on Algeria, in English. That makes it fun to play beside a recording made in the region itself: two different ways of telling the same place. The disc was digitized by the Library of Congress for its National Jukebox, and because it was published in 1909 it is now in the public domain, free for anyone to play and share.

Fatenah (2009) is a Palestinian animated short, and it opens with a quiet line: "Inspired by a true story." Ahmad Habash directed it and handled the animation and photography; Saed Andoni co-wrote the screenplay with Habash and Ambrogio Manenti, and also produced and edited; Said Murad wrote the music. Our record describes it as a story of a woman facing illness in Gaza. What makes it a find is the pairing: a story from real life, told through animation. If you've watched a festival short that left you thoughtful for the rest of the evening, this lives in the same neighbourhood. It's in Arabic, it's free to watch on the Internet Archive, and it's shared under a CC BY-NC-ND licence, so you can enjoy it and send it along.

Imagine opening a drawer and finding film of the Hajj from around 1939–40, the season the title calls 1360–1361H. This clip runs 4 minutes 21 seconds, in a 1080p digital copy that someone uploaded to Wikimedia Commons in 2019. The page lists its author as unknown, which is part of its charm. Today, the Hajj reaches us through phone videos and livestreams, so a pilgrimage seen through footage nearly ninety years old has a particular glow. It invites the small, happy game of looking at everything that is not the main event: clothing, the pace of walking, how people stand together. The file is in the public domain (Saudi Arabia's copyright terms for works published before 1979 have expired), so it can be shown freely. Watch it with a quiet room and no hurry.

Here is Rumi doing something very human: telling you about a musician. In "The Harper," from Book I of the Mesnevi, a minstrel from the days of 'Umer is so gifted that nightingales weep with joy, applause breaks like thunder, and "his made the saddest gay." Rumi compares his voice to Isrāfīl, the angel whose trumpet blast, a footnote explains, will wake the dead, and then adds a tender line: "Dear friend to Isrāfīl he was, and mendicant." It's a lovely reminder that music has been trusted to lift people for a very long time. You can hear its echo any time a song changes the mood of a whole room. This version is James W. Redhouse's 1881 English translation, in rhyming couplets (part of Trübner's Oriental Series), and it's free on Project Gutenberg. Read a few lines aloud; the rhymes are fun.

This one is a little time capsule: the Lebanese-born novelist and journalist Hanan al-Shaykh on NPR's Fresh Air, on 17 February 1994. She was talking about The Story of Zahra, which had just come out in the United States from Anchor Books. NPR's description says several Arab countries had banned the book since its original publication fourteen years earlier, and that it follows a contemporary Lebanese woman making her way through family life in war-ravaged Beirut. Her novel Women of Sand and Myrrh had arrived in the US the year before. Books can have long lives: here is a novel meeting a new readership across an ocean, with its author talking it through on the radio. If you've ever picked up a book because you heard its author speak, you know the feeling. Start with the interview page, then see where it leads you.

Some books explain how an idea moved. This one, by the Iranian activist Noushin Ahmadi Khorasani, is an insider's account of the One Million Signatures Campaign for the Reform of Discriminatory Laws, published in 2009 by Women's Learning Partnership. The description calls the campaign "democratic, nonhierarchical, open, and evolving," and credits much of its energy to constant, searching discussion: a core group of experienced activists staying open to the views of thousands of younger women who joined, often at considerable personal risk. The surprise is how familiar the lesson feels. Anyone who has helped run a school committee or a volunteer group knows that people stay when they are heard. The book also touches on family law topics such as polygamy and mahr, so read it as one participant's view of a debated subject. It lives on the Internet Archive.

A snapshot from October 1999: zabihah.com, "your guide to halal restaurants," and its front page leads with a cheesesteak. The page reprints a Philadelphia Inquirer story of July 27, 1999, about Atiq Chaudhry, a Pakistani immigrant whose Pizza Pak II hoagie shop kept getting Muslim customers asking for halal meat. His answer was a halal cheesesteak, and the page says the response was overwhelming. Under it, the founders explain themselves: born and raised in America, they love "curries from Pakistan, tajines from Morocco, Islamic Chinese," and wanted a place to share where to eat. Reviews come from "people like you," and the page honestly adds that there is no official authority to verify claims, so please check for yourself. If you have ever trusted a friend's restaurant tip over a star rating, this is where that habit meets the early web.

In 2004, a volunteer project called Arabeyes set out to make the Unix/Linux world fully speak Arabic, and its archived front page reads like a lively community noticeboard. Volunteers from all over contribute: one update reports a fix for a bug that affected some 'Asr prayer-time calculations in certain parts of the world; another celebrates a landmark goal, the first fully Arabized installer in a major Linux distribution. My favourite detail: the person they salute for that effort, Christian Perrier, is described as a non-Arabic speaker who helped anyway. On December 18, 2004, at the Casablanca GNU/Linux Days in Morocco, Arabeyes received a "Best Free/Open Project" award presented by Richard Stallman. It is a small, cheerful portrait of people building tools for their own language, one patch at a time.

In 1999 an amateur-astronomy website put the crescent moon on a map. "Moonsighting with Astronomy" posted a visibility curve for the new moon due on December 7, 1999 at 22:32 UT, and explained that on December 8 it would not be visible in the Middle East, and in North America only with perfect conditions and "a good binocular." If someone saw it there, the first day of fasting would be December 9. The site rests on a criterion by Khalid Shaukat, built from over 900 observations gathered across 150 years, and says its predictions had held up almost every month since 1993 (that is the site's own claim). The page also uses MoonCalc 5.0 with Yallop's criteria. It's a delightful meeting of old-fashioned looking-up-at-the-sky and a very early web page full of maps and numbers. Looking for the crescent at dusk to begin Ramadan is a practice many people still keep.

A falcon strikes a water bird, and the potter holds the moment still. This dish was made in Syria in the 1100s, in the lakabi style. The design is carved into the surface. Raised outlines keep glazes of different colours from running together. The body is fritware, a white ceramic made mostly of quartz with a little crushed glass and fine clay. The museum says Chinese porcelain probably influenced it. Falconry was a favourite sport of Muslim rulers for centuries. The Cleveland Museum of Art notes that the Qur'an sanctions it (5:4–6). The dish is about 40 centimetres across, wide and shallow. The whole hunt fits on one plate.

Tiny painted scenes, on a cup you can hold in one hand. This beaker comes from Kashan, Iran, and dates to between 1180 and 1220, in the Seljuq period. It is mina'i ware, from the Persian word for enamel. The museum calls mina'i the first true polychrome ceramic, with blues, greens and purples against sharp black and red. Its scenes often recall book illustrations: rows of seated courtiers, enthroned rulers, hunting and falconry. This one shows seated princes. A band of Kufic script runs around the outside, and another around the inside. The beaker is about 13 centimetres tall. It belongs to the Cleveland Museum of Art.

A long-necked lute that has clearly travelled. The Cleveland Museum of Art says this tanbūr, collected in Ottoman Syria in the late 1800s, has Syrian, Turkish and Iranian traits. It is a neat picture of music moving between cultures. The instrument is ancient. The museum compares it to lutes used in Pharaonic Egypt and Mesopotamia. In its many forms the tanbūr was common across the Islamic world, often played solo in both sacred and secular settings. Burn marks decorate the pear-shaped body. Inlaid dots of mother-of-pearl may also have helped the player find their place on the fret board. It has two pairs of wire strings, played with a quill plectrum.

Seventeen books, and this is the fifth. İbrahim Müteferrika's press in Istanbul, which the catalogue calls the first Turkish press, printed 17 works between 1729 and 1742. This is number five: Tarih-i Timur Gürkân, a history of Timur. The credits list Ibn ʻArabshāh (1392–1450) and Nazmizade Murtaza, with Müteferrika as printer. He also wrote a preface and index. It is Turkish in Arabic script, 129 leaves, about 21 centimetres tall. This copy was digitized by McGill University Library and is in the public domain. You can page through a very early printed book, from a very short list.

Rumi, in conversation. This is a conversation between Krista Tippett and Fatemeh Keshavarz, recorded on January 17, 2007, for the radio programme On Being. The show page calls Rumi a 13th-century Muslim mystic and poet. It says he has long shaped Muslims around the world and has now become popular in the West. It adds that he created a new language of love within the Sufi tradition. The conversation goes into his world and listens for its echoes in ours, with his poetry along the way. This is the unedited interview, posted to the Internet Archive in 2012. The finished version aired as "The Ecstatic Faith of Rumi." Good listening for a long walk.

An empire's official newspaper, in its own pages. Takvim-i Vekayi was the official newspaper of the Ottoman Empire. Commons also gives its French name, Journal officiel de l'empire ottoman. This is issue No. 773, dated 6 November 1864. It carries the "Constitutive law of the department formed under the name of vilayet of the Danube," printed in Ottoman Turkish. The scan comes from the Ankara University newspaper database, and the file is in the public domain. It is a primary source in the plainest sense: a government notice, in the form readers saw it.

Light, written in glazed tile. This prayer niche, or mihrab, is ceramic mosaic in the style of Safavid Isfahan, Iran. The museum dates it to the 1500s or the mid-1900s. A mihrab is the focal point of a mosque, set in the wall that faces Mecca. Qur'anic verses in thuluth script surround it, in white glaze. Behind them runs an arabesque vine in gold, turquoise and green, a colour the museum associates with paradise. The text is from the Chapter of Light: "His Light is like a niche in which is a lamp." A niche carries words about a niche. The mihrab stands about 2.9 metres tall. It is at the Cleveland Museum of Art.

A mosque built in two stages. The Al-Ashrafiah Mosque in Taiz, Yemen, is described as the peak of Rasulid religious architecture. The first stage dates to around 1297, under Ashraf I. The second came between 1376 and 1400, under Ashraf II. The prayer hall is backed by identical minarets. Above it, eight small cupolas surround one large dome. The ceilings are richly carved and decorated. The description comes from the Yemenna forum and was saved to the Internet Archive. It tells you what to look for before you ever see the building: two minarets, a ring of small domes, and carved ceilings.

Four minarets, built to mark the end of a plague. This page from a 2004 Hyderabad tourism site describes the Charminar. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built it in 1591 to commemorate the end of the plague. The plan is a square, 20 metres on each side, with four grand arches 11 metres wide. The four-storey minarets rise 20 metres from the roof and measure 24 metres from the plinth. A mosque with 45 prayer spaces sits in the western part of the roof, with a large open space in front for Friday prayers. The page also tours nearby places, including Golconda Fort and Mecca Masjid, which it calls the city's biggest mosque.

Friday-night football, run by a mosque community. This small web page keeps the score. The BUJU Boys (over 18) and The Usual Suspects (under 18) play each other. All the players belong to the Stanmore mosque, and matches take place at Alperton Goals, usually during school holidays. The tally: five wins for the BUJU Boys, two for the Usual Suspects. Stanmore FC also entered a five-a-side league there, on Fridays at 6.30, for under-21s. The page records that the league had ended, the team finished second, and trophies would be given out in September. It also has a joke page and a news page. Local sport, kept with care.

A workout with drums. In this 2015 video, the filmmaker, posting as Oxlaey, visits a zurkhaneh in a suburb of Tehran. Zurkhaneh, also called Pahlevani, is a traditional Iranian power workout. The drums push everyone to go a little further. It combines martial arts, aerobics and a few yoga-like moves. The club had men of all ages. What the visitor remembers most is how members supported each other. They greeted one another, caught each other if they were spinning out of control, and handed out dry towels. The filmmaker calls it a communal activity, built on the social structure of the neighbourhood, unlike the individual workout of a Western gym. The clip is shared under CC BY-SA 3.0.

Oil wrestling, in a sultan's garden. This watercolour shows güres, Turkish oil wrestling, in the gardens of Topkapı Palace. An anonymous Greek artist painted it around 1809. It belongs to an album of Ottoman costumes and scenes at the V&A in London (museum number D.115-1895), and the image is in the public domain. Commons files it under "Oil wrestling in Turkey." Another record in this collection shows an oil wrestling tournament in Istanbul on 6 August 2006. You can set the painting beside a photograph taken nearly two centuries later.

In the early 1950s, Egypt invited a camera into its film studios. This short film, probably from 1951, was produced by the Hamilton Wright Organization for the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. At 0:50 you meet Samia Gamal, a dancer and film actress. At 1:15 a director, standing beside a Mitchell 35mm camera, gives her direction. Then comes Studio Misr, set up in 1934 by the economist Talaat Harb. It was owned and staffed by Egyptians and known as "The Studio of Egypt." Its first film was Wedad (1936), the first to star the singer Umm Kulthum. The narrator says Egypt had 226 movie theatres and that Arabic-speaking audiences want their own films. Around 4:28, an Egyptian western is being filmed.

A factory tour, narrated in Arabic. This ten-minute film follows Coca-Cola bottling in the Middle East. The Internet Archive's description says it shows sports and leisure, the making of bottles, and how industries such as glass and bag manufacturing work together to supply the bottling plant. It also shows modern production techniques, with an emphasis on purity and quality. The record gives no date. The film sits in the Prelinger collection under a public-domain licence. Press play and watch the bottles go by.

A caliph, standing, on a gold coin. This dinar of the Umayyad Caliph ʻAbd al-Malik was struck in 74–77 AH, in the 690s. It is known as the "Caliphal Image" or "Standing Caliph" solidus. Its design is based on Byzantine coin traditions. The photographer, PHGCOM, shot it at the British Museum, and the image is in the public domain. The description adds a note: there are official representations of the human figure in the Islamic context, and the figure here is the caliph himself. A related coin of 75 AH (694–695 CE) reads "khalifa of God, Commander of the Faithful." It is a coin built on a familiar format, with a new inscription.

A coin that speaks two languages. This gold dinar was struck in al-Andalus, in Spain, and dated 98 AH (716–717 AD), in the reign of Sulaiman. It weighs 4.16 grams. Around the edge, the Latin reads "Feritos Solidus in Spania," with a year in Roman numerals. The outer margin in Arabic reads "bismillah, struck was this dinar in al-Andalus in the year eight and ninety." At the centre is an eight-pointed star with "Muhammad rasul Allah" across two lines. The auction house that sold it, CNG, calls it "a very rare and early bilingual dinar of Muslim Spain." It notes that a similar one sold at Sotheby's on 12 July 1993 for £19,800. Two writing systems, one small gold coin.

Cairo's great market, in one frame. Khan el-Khalili is a famous bazaar and souq in the historic centre of Cairo. It was established as a trading centre in the Mamluk era and is named for one of its several historic caravanserais. Today, the description says, the bazaar district is one of Cairo's main attractions for tourists and Egyptians alike. This photograph is by Mohammed Moussa, taken on 11 February 2019, for Wiki Loves Monuments 2020 in Egypt. It is a large file, 4603 by 4000 pixels, shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. Zoom in and take your time.

An instrument made of two eras. This brass planispheric astrolabe is held at the Arab World Institute in Paris (AI 86-45). The mother and the tympan come from Ottoman Turkey, 1098 AH, which is 1686–87. The spider, the cut-out top plate that maps the stars, was made in the Maghreb around 1850, more than 160 years later. The brass is engraved and incised, and the whole piece is just 10.2 centimetres across. Commons files it under "Astrolabes of the Islamic Golden Age." The photograph, by Pom², is shared under CC BY-SA 3.0.

A candle that tells the time, drawn with care. This folio shows "The Scribe Candle Clock" from a copy of al-Jazari's treatise on automata, Kitāb fī maʿrifat al-ḥiyal al-handasiyya, "The book of knowledge of ingenious mechanical devices." Al-Jazari died in 1206. This copy is dated Ramadan 715, which is December 1315. The page shows the candle clock on one side, with text on the other. The manuscript is in the Topkapı Palace Museum, and the image is in the public domain. The page is engineering explained as a picture.

A body, drawn in colour, around 1384. Manṣūr ibn Muḥammad ibn Ilyās came from a family of physicians and scholars in Shiraz. His best-known work, Tashrīḥ-i Manṣūrī, or "Manṣūr's anatomy," contains the earliest surviving Islamic anatomical illustrations of the whole human body. They include full-page figures, drawn in pen with several colours of ink. The chapters cover bones, nerves, muscles, veins and arteries, then compound organs such as the heart and brain. One figure shows the arterial system of a pregnant woman. He dedicated the work to Sultan Pīr Muḥammad, a grandson of Timur. This copy was made in 1709 and now sits in the Cushing collection at Yale.

A surgeon's book that travelled for centuries. Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013), known in the West as Albucasis, was born in Zahra, near Cordoba. He is regarded as one of the greatest Arab physicians, strong in internal medicine, surgery and eye care. His encyclopedia, the Al-Tasreef, covers surgery, orthopedics, pharmacology and nutrition. It describes more than 300 diseases and over 200 surgical instruments. In the 12th century, Gerard of Cremona translated the surgery section into Latin. The translation became a medical textbook in Europe, referenced by physicians into the late 18th century. This is the first printed Latin edition, published in Augsburg in 1519. The Arabic version was printed in London in 1778 and in India in 1918.

A doctor's handbook, dedicated to a governor. Abu Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–925), a Persian physician, philosopher and alchemist, wrote the Kitab al-Mansouri in the early 10th century. He lived in Rayy for at least 30 years and became director of its hospital. He later directed a hospital in Baghdad. The book is dedicated to Rayy's governor, al-Mansur ibn Ishāq, and has ten chapters. The first six cover diet, hygiene, anatomy, physiology, pathology and surgery. The last four turn practical, from diagnosis to therapy. In the late 12th century, Gherardo da Cremona translated it into Latin in Toledo. The manuscript here has red headings and marginal notes, including a long one in Amharic letters near the start.

A mosque reopens, and a photographer is there. In 1990, Danny Lev photographed the first Friday service at the Hassan Bek Mosque, near the sea between Tel Aviv and Jaffa, after years of renovation. The Tel Aviv municipality had declared the mosque unsafe after its minaret collapsed. Over ten years it was restored brick by brick. The caption notes that the Muslim community complained the Ministry of Religious Affairs and the municipality had not given enough funds. The municipality, for its part, accused the mosque's religious committee of neglecting the building. In the end, money was found and the mosque was rededicated. The record comes from the National Library of Israel through Europeana, under CC BY 4.0. It is a small story about who looks after a shared building.

A dance, painted outside the city. This Rijksmuseum painting, made around 1720 to 1737, shows Greek men and women dancing the khorra in the countryside outside Istanbul. The museum adds a note about the painter, Vanmour. Because he was not Muslim, it was easier for him to reach the Greek community in Istanbul than the Turkish side of life. The image carries the Public Domain Mark, so anyone can use it. It is a scene of everyday life, painted by someone who had access.

A song from Beirut, February 11, 1909. The label names Salmo Effendi El-Midani of Damascus as the singer. The Gramophone Company recorded him in Beirut. The disc is a 10-inch record, catalogue number G.C.-10-12118. The song is "Dizzeit Bistam Hajrak," listed as a Syrian male song. The label mentions Anton al-Shawa's famous takht ensemble. The other side carries "Ya Min Ilaik Ilawalem." The Great 78 Project digitized the disc, and the Internet Archive page lets you play it, under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence. You can hear a voice from more than a century ago.

A global contest to document Ramadan, explained in a conference talk. This video is from the ESEAP Conference 2026 (video dated 15 May 2026). Organisers describe how to run the Wiki Loves Ramadan campaign across the ESEAP region. The description calls Wiki Loves Ramadan an annual global contest to document and share the customs and traditions observed during the month. The aim is a comprehensive, multilingual body of knowledge about Ramadan. It would show how differently the month is observed around the world, and strengthen the presence of Islamic communities on Wikimedia projects, including Wikipedia. The campaign is described as new, and the talk also looks at the 2025 edition in the region. The video is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0.

A 1999 link list, tended by hand. This GeoCities page begins with an apology and a plan. The owner, writing as UmHajar, is too busy to revise the links section and is slowly deleting the old bad links. What remains is a map of the early web. Sections cover the Qur'an, scholars, women and marriage, books and bookstores, Islamic centres, magazines, personal homepages and art. It points to an Arabic-learning program, to Rafed Net ("very large site in Arabic and English"), and to Hawzah.net in Farsi and English. A Qur'an section lists translations in French, German, Dutch, Farsi, Spanish, Italian, Swahili, Turkish and Chinese. There is even an audio guide to the words to say when you pray. Before feeds and follows, this is how people shared what they found.

A webring, a clubhouse of websites. This 1997 page explains the al-Shi'a WebRing, a ring for web developers engaged in Shi'a electronic publishing. Members join to promote publishing within their school of thought, to exchange experiences, and to reach agreement on the best technologies to use. The ringmaster includes only "exceptionally informative" Shi'a sites. It is free to join. The sign-up form asks for a site title, a URL, up to 20 keywords and a short description. A second form edits your entry later. There is also a place to get the code and images for your own page. A scrolling marquee welcomes visitors. It is early social networking in a small, well-organised form.

A scarf, and a school debate. In this essay, Nakata Khaula, a Japanese woman, recalls the fierce debate in France about girls wearing hijab at school. She writes that most people seemed to feel the head-scarf conflicted with the idea that state-funded schools be neutral about religion. She could not see why there was such a fuss over "such a small thing as a scarf." In her view, schools could accommodate students' religious practice as long as it did not disrupt the school day. She links the debate to unemployment and worries about immigration. She notes that more young women in Arab countries were wearing hijab than many expected. In Japan, she adds, it may be read as conservative traditionalism. The essay is on a Muslim student association site. It is her view, set out plainly.

A loom, a rhythm and a long pattern. This short video was filmed in Guediawaye, a suburb of Dakar, Senegal. It shows a weaver making a textile called Seurou Rabal. He moves the loom with practised movements, interweaving vibrant threads. The uploader says the techniques are centuries old and passed down through generations. The clip was uploaded in March 2024 by Wuzyprod as part of Wiki Loves Africa 2024. It is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0, and Commons files it under weavers and artisans at work. Put it on full screen.

The last Egyptian kiswah, remembered in one curtain. This photograph shows the sitara, the curtain for the door of the Kaaba, from the last Egyptian-made kiswah. The description says it was made in 1381 AH, before Saudi Arabia took over making the kiswah. Ahmed Naji took the picture on 24 July 2022, and it is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. It is a large file, 6000 by 8000 pixels, so you can study the textile closely when you zoom in. A craft tradition, at the moment it passed from one place to another, in a single image.

The moon, phase by phase. This illustration of the phases of the moon comes from a manuscript of the Kitāb al-Tafhīm by al-Bīrūnī (973–1048). Commons dates the copy to the 18th century. The scan was made from Seyyed Hossein Nasr's Islamic Science: An Illustrated Study (1976), and the image is in the public domain. It is a simple page with a clear idea: the moon changes shape, and a drawing can show how.

A calendar you can unroll. This item is a scroll in the Wellcome Collection, MS Ottoman Turkish 3, containing a perpetual calendar with illuminated sections. It is a Ruzname-i dairevi: astronomical tables for both the Arabic (Islamic) and Rumi (Julian) calendars. They give a chronological account of seasonal change, the sun's entry into the signs of the zodiac, and sunset times. The calendar is written in the style of Süleyman Hikmeti, who died after 1828. He was imam of Istanbul's Cedid Ali Pasha mosque and taught calligraphy at the Lali-zade Abdülkadir Efendi school. The scroll's images are shared under CC BY 4.0. One object holds time, season and handwriting together.

A museum builder who also wrote history. This open-access article from 2024, in the journal El Tarikh, is about Fuat Sezgin and how he wrote the history of science in the Islamic world. It says he is popular among researchers in Indonesia for his critical studies of hadith, but his work on the history of science gets less attention. The authors give three reasons his contribution matters. He continued and complemented earlier scholars such as Carl Brockelmann and Helmut Ritter. He presented authoritative primary sources for philological study of manuscripts. And he did not stop at theory. He established a museum and an institution devoted to the study of Islamic science.

A small book from Timbuktu, about the pillars of faith. Timbuktu, in today's Mali, was founded around 1100 as a trading centre across the Sahara. From the 14th century it was also an important seat of Islamic learning. Its libraries hold manuscripts in many styles of Arabic script. This one is Al-Jawāhir al-Ḥisan, "The beautiful jewels for edification in the Pillars of the Faith," by Arbāb al-Kharṭūmī. It covers belief in God, his angels and messengers, and the scriptures. It also discusses the last judgment and the inevitability of God's will. The World Digital Library dates the manuscript between 1500 and 1900, and the scan is in the public domain. A trading city could also be a reading city.

A garden laid out like a plan. Humayun's Tomb garden sits near the Yamuna river in Delhi. Babur, Humayun's father, is credited with bringing the Persian chahar bagh, the four-part garden, to India. Humayun's garden is described as a geometrically perfect example of the type, with one difference: it has a building at its centre. That makes the garden a setting for a building, not a place enjoyed from a pavilion. It symbolises the emperor's place in paradise. A grid of water channels and paths divides it into 36 squares. It was not the first of its kind, but it is the oldest to survive in good condition. The Aga Khan Trust funded a restoration, and by 2003 water was again flowing in the channels and fountains.

Two sentries, an avenue of trees, and a garden with a long history. This photograph by John Burke, taken between 1878 and 1880, shows the Afghan amir's garden in Jalālābād. It comes from an album of rare photographs linked to the Second Anglo-Afghan War. Babur, the first Mughal emperor, chose the site of modern Jalālābād. Building began in 1560 under his grandson Akbar, who oversaw many gardens in the city. Many Mughal gardens followed the Persian chahar bagh, "four gardens," which divides a garden into four sections by water or straight paths. In the picture, the sentries stand beside an avenue of trees that leads to a circular summerhouse in the middle distance. The image is in the public domain, from the World Digital Library.

A long pool, lined with fountains. The Patio de la Acequia, or Court of the Long Pond, is one of the most popular parts of the Generalife gardens at the Alhambra in Granada. The pool is 48 metres long. Andrew Dunn took this photograph on 11 May 2006. It is a portrait-format image, 665 by 1024 pixels, shared under CC BY-SA 2.0. Other records in this collection explain the chahar bagh, the four-part garden with water channels. This one shows the same love of water in a different place.

Ramadan, explained to kids. This GeoCities page from 2001 tells the story plainly. Ramadan is the month the Qur'an was given to the Prophet Muhammad, through the angel Jibril, over 23 years. Families fast during daylight hours, and instead of feeding their bodies they pray and read the Qur'an. They also try not to say or listen to anything harmful. The page says it reminds them of people who may not have enough to eat. Each morning begins with Suhur, a meal eaten together before the Fajr prayer. Even young children fast a few days, and many kids give up favourite foods or bad habits. The page adds that Muslims are supposed to read the entire Qur'an during the month. A clear, friendly lesson.

A study group, started online. This early-web page, "Tools for Studying Islamic Studies," says its authors compiled information for people who are considering Islam, have recently embraced it, or are helping someone who is. The page also welcomes any Muslim sister, or any woman interested in studying Islam, to join. To do so, you send an email to the webmistress and join the network. The page lives on a GeoCities site for South Dakota Muslim women. It is short. You can still see the shape of an early online community: a clear purpose, an open invitation, and one person holding the door.

A lecture in Urdu, saved from a livestream. On 9 January 2011, Maulana Wahiduddin Khan, president of the Islamic Center in New Delhi, gave a talk titled "The Role of Islam in History" on Ustream. The Internet Archive's description calls him an Islamic scholar and thinker, and the lecture "thought provoking." The recording runs about 74 minutes. It is available as MP3 and Ogg audio. It is tagged with Islam, religion, peace and interfaith, and it carries a CC0 licence, so anyone can share it. An hour and a quarter to settle into, in the original language.

A palace kitchen, from the inside. The caption says the imperial kitchens at Topkapı Palace prepared a large variety of meals for a single person. A team of twelve cooks, guided by the chief cook, did the work. The chief cook was also responsible for the porcelain tableware used at the Emperor's table and when foreign ambassadors were received. This photograph, taken on 15 March 2019 by Zara1992, shows the utensils used in the Ottoman kitchen. It is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. The details are the point: twelve cooks, one diner, and a chief cook who also looked after the plates.

A grocery list, made by a community. The Islamic Association of Nagoya published this list of halal foods in Japan. They made it by writing to food companies, to avoid eating haram meat and alcohol hidden in ingredients. For fast food, the group checked whether items were cooked with lard or other animal oil. The list names trade names for instant noodles, soy sauce, miso and vinegar. The page is on GeoCities, saved from the early web. An ordinary problem, solved with persistence: a few people ask questions of companies, collect the answers, and share them with the next shopper.

A 1999 web guide to Iran. This travel page counts visitors since 21 July 1999 and was updated on 8 August 2000. It recommends two guidebooks: an Odyssey series guide to Iran (2nd edition, October 1999) and the Lonely Planet Guide to Iran (2nd edition, 1998). There is also a track to listen to, the Dastgah of Homayoun played on the ney by Hassan Kassayi. It is about 540 KB, which the page says takes four minutes to download on a 56K modem. The index covers travelogues, photo collections, attractions, maps, cuisine, hotels, history, and arts and culture. It quotes Condé Nast Traveller (May 2000): "Iran is, without any doubt at all, the warmest, politest, most hospitable country that I have ever been in – almost shamingly so."

A city that was once a lake. This page describes Konya, in Turkey. It says the whole Konya basin was a lake 18,000 years ago, and that the Romans called the city Iconium, "the city of icons." Today it is a place of pilgrimage, because Rumi, the leader of the Mevlevis, is buried there. The Mevlana Museum has been a museum since 1926. In its courtyard are dervish cells and kitchens. Under the green dome lies a blue marble sarcophagus for Mevlana and his son Sultan Veled, a gift from Suleyman the Magnificent. A cloth with Qur'an verses in gold thread covers it, a gift of Sultan Abdulhamit II in 1894. The hall of the Sema ceremony holds instruments: ney, rebab, tef and tambur.

Orion, drawn the way it looks on a globe. This page comes from al-Sufi's Book of the Fixed Stars, a revision of Ptolemy's Almagest with Arabic star names and drawings of the constellations. The manuscript is dated 1009–10 (AH 400). It is held at the Bodleian Libraries in Oxford (MS. Marsh 144). Orion is al-jabbār, "the giant." The picture shows Orion as it would appear on a celestial globe. That is the mirror image of how an observer sees it from the earth. Al-Sufi gave each constellation two illustrations, one for each view. The image is shared under CC BY 4.0.

A brass sky, in the shape of a ball. This large Persian celestial globe carries an ascription to Hadi Isfahani and is dated 1197 AH, which is 1782–83. It is a sphere of brass, engraved with markings, figures and astrological symbols, with inscriptions throughout. The photograph, by Muhammadahmad79, was uploaded in July 2016 and is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. It sits well beside the Orion page in this collection, which explains how a constellation looks on a globe compared with the real sky. Between them, the idea is clear: the stars, laid out on a sphere.

A water clock, with the mechanism hidden. This is a model of al-Jazari's goblet clepsydra, from around 1200. It is displayed at the Istanbul Museum of the History of Science and Technology in Islam. The description says its sophisticated, water-powered mechanism is hidden inside. A clepsydra is a timepiece that measures time by the regulated flow of liquid into or out of a vessel. Water clocks, along with sundials, are likely among the oldest time-measuring instruments. Dosseman took the photograph on 1 June 2014, and it is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. The clever part is out of sight.

A rainbow, worked out with a diagram. Kamāl al-Dīn al-Fārisī (1267–1319) wrote the Tanqīḥ al-Manāẓir, a revision and commentary on Ibn al-Haytham's book on optics, the Kitāb al-Manāẓir. This page, from around 1300, shows his construction of the primary and secondary rainbows. The manuscript is in Leiden University Library (Or. 201, f. 290a). The text is in Arabic, the book runs to 636 pages, and the digitized page is in the public domain. Ibn al-Haytham died in 1038, and al-Fārisī was writing around 1300, building on his book. A field hands a question forward, and a diagram asks how a rainbow is made.

A door, scanned in 3D. This record comes from Tech4Heritage, which made a glTF 3D model of a wooden door from Old Mosul in 2021. The description places Old Mosul on the west bank of the Tigris, opposite the remains of ancient Nineveh. It says the city's history goes back to the early second millennium BC. Its architecture is mostly marked by the Middle Ages, from the 12th to the 19th century, with Ottoman buildings especially notable among religious and cultural ones. This is one of the surviving wooden doors, a style mostly used for the main doors of buildings, decorated with plant and geometric patterns. The model is shared under CC BY 4.0, so you can turn the door around.

A mosque tour, led by the man who looks after it. This video was filmed on 31 May 2025 at the Mahmud al-Numa Mosque, near Faruq Street in Mosul, Iraq. The man in the video is Abu Saqar al-Qassab, the mosque's caretaker. The record says the building lay in ruins for decades before it was restored in 2024. So the walk-through shows a building restored only in 2024. The clip is in full HD, 1920 by 1080, and shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. It is a good companion to the 3D model of a wooden Mosul door in this collection. One shows a single object up close. This shows a whole building, with its caretaker beside you.
